Abstract This study aims to evaluate the impact of digital technology adoption on efficiency, transparency and accountability in zakat management, with a focus on the younger generation and highly educated individuals. Using quantitative analysis of 400 respondents in Tangerang city, the findings show that digital zakat adoption is more dominant among the 18–34 age group and respondents with a bachelor’s degree or higher education. This group is more prepared to use digital platforms because of better access to technology and a greater understanding of its benefits. However, digital literacy gaps and limited access remain major challenges, particularly for older adults and low-income communities. The findings highlight that technology adoption, zakat ecosystem strengthening, and community involvement significantly influence operational efficiency and transparency in zakat management. This research contributes to the literature on zakat digitalization and offers strategic recommendations for zakat institutions to optimize technology adoption, emphasizing an inclusive approach that considers the demographic characteristics of users. Collaboration among zakat institutions, the government, and technology providers is essential to ensure successful technology integration and to meet the public’s demand for more transparent and efficient zakat services. Research shows that the application of digital technology in zakat management significantly improves operational efficiency by automating previous manual processes (Buana et al., 2022; Hassan & Muneeza, 2023). Through digital integration platforms in the zakat collection process, institutions can achieve a faster and more coordinated approach, thereby reducing traditional bureaucratic inefficiencies (Musari, 2022; Uddin & Sultana, 2022). Technologies such as e-wallets, payment applications, and cloud-based management systems accelerate transactions, improve fund cycles, and lower operational costs by reducing reliance on human resources and physical assets (Haider et al., 2024). Research also highlights that these technologies not only improve efficiency but also make a major contribution to the disposal of zakat management by increasing the accuracy of zakat distribution to mustahik in a timely manner (Mohammed et al., 2021; Mutamimah et al., 2021; Nazeri et al., 2023). Thus, the application of digital technology not only supports efficiency and transparency but also becomes the basis for ensuring that there is no mismanagement of zakat in the future. Methodology This study employs a quantitative methodology (Neuman, 2017), which is conducted in Kota Tangerang and comprises 13 subdistricts with a total population of 1,930,556 residents. The sample size was determined via the Slovin formula with a 5% margin of error, resulting in a total of 400 respondents. The probability sampling technique utilized was simple random sampling, ensuring that each individual within the population had an equal likelihood of being selected as a participant (Bungin, 2005). https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Arwen et al. (2026) 6 Simple random sampling was chosen because it provides an equal opportunity for every individual in the population to be selected. This method ensures unbiased representation of various segments in the population, allowing for a diverse sample that can accurately reflect community involvement in digital zakat management. Given that the purpose of this study is to capture a comprehensive view of technology adoption in zakat, this technique is the most effective technique for ensuring that all demographic groups are proportionally represented. The respondents were selected randomly, with a focus on individuals who had experience with or were aware of the digital zakat platform in the past 12 months. To ensure representativeness, respondents were selected proportionally in 13 subdistricts in Tangerang city. This approach helps ensure that the data reflect relevant user experiences in the digital zakat ecosystem. Primary data collection methods were conducted through the distribution of questionnaires to chosen respondents, as well as direct observation and interviews with relevant participants to ensure a thorough understanding of the subject matter (Snijkers et al., 2013). The questionnaire was designed to measure various aspects related to the application of technological advances in zakat, including technology adoption, operational efficiency, and perceived levels of transparency and accountability. To ensure the validity and reliability of the research instrument, a prerequisite test was conducted. Furthermore, to address potential common method bias (CMB), this study implemented several procedural improvements during the questionnaire design and data collection stages, including respondent anonymity, randomization of question order, and assurance of confidentiality. In addition, Harman's single-factor test was conducted, and the results revealed that no single factor explained most of the variance, indicating that CMB did not pose a significant threat to the validity of this study. Results The embrace of technological advancements offers a significant opportunity to enhance both efficiency and transparency. Digital platforms streamline collection and distribution processes, expedite operations and increase accessibility to a broader segment of society. However, as with any technological advancement, certain challenges must be addressed to ensure smooth adoption of zakat technology platforms across all societal levels. A thorough understanding of the demographic characteristics of digital zakat users is essential for tailoring technological developments to meet the specific needs and capabilities of the community. Respondents' income has also been proven to affect their perception of the zakat ecosystem, community engagement, and transparency and accountability of zakat institutions (Chotib et al., 2023; Sawandi & Aziz, 2020). The respondents with middle and high incomes showed a greater tendency to pay attention to aspects of transparency and accountability, which are very important for ensuring the sustainability of public trust in zakat institutions (Harrison & Sayogo, 2014; Muliansyah et al., 2022). These findings are in line with the research of Ahuja et al., who reported that individuals with higher incomes are considerably more concerned about reporting and clarity in the use of social funds (Ahuja et al., 2023). However, experience using technology has proven to have a significant influence on the embrace of digital advancements in zakat platforms, suggesting that those with greater experience tend to be more comfortable using digital platforms for zakat payments (Ninglasari, 2021; Salleh & Chowdhury, 2020b). The analysis shows that digital platforms such as mobile applications tend to be more effective in increasing public engagement than websites that function only as a means of information (Bonina et al., 2021; Lovejoy & Saxton, 2012). This finding supports the theory of digital interactivity, which states that interactive features such as notifications can encourage users to be more actively engaged in social activities (Scardovi, 2017; Thottoli et al., 2023). This research is consistent with previous studies on the adoption of technology in the Islamic finance sector (Azizah, 2023; Oladapo et al., 2022), but it also offers some differences that are important to note. Razzak's study revealed that the adoption of digital technology in the Islamic finance sector has great potential to improve efficiency and transparency (Razzak et al., 2024). However, this study broadens the understanding by examining the specific impact of digital platforms on zakat management in Indonesia, which is still limited to the local context. Compared with research by Utami et al., which highlighted the importance of digital literacy in the adoption of zakat technology (Utami et al., 2020), while digital literacy is important, the experience of using technology directly has a greater impact on the embrace of digital advancements in zakat platforms, a key factor in building a sustainable digital ecosystem (Nuraini & Budiandru, 2023; Syarif, 2024). Digital transformation has a significant influence on improving efficiency and accountability in the philanthropic sector (George & Schillebeeckx, 2022; Rasidb et al., 2021; Utami et al., 2020). However, the study also revealed that while technology benefits the speed of the zakat collection process, in some cases, the adoption of technology can actually reduce efficiency, particularly in circumstances where digital infrastructure is not adequately developed or where user adaptation is still insufficient. This is in line with the findings of Abidin and Utami, who stated that the main challenge in the application of digital technology in philanthropy is the readiness of infrastructure and user adaptation (Abidin & Utami, 2020). The drawback of this study is the lack of an in-depth approach to the challenges of digital literacy experienced by older age groups and low-income communities, and previous studies have shown that the digital divide is a major factor hindering the adoption of technological advancements (Ahmad & Yahaya, 2023; Beik et al., 2021; Salleh & Chowdhury, 2020b). On the other hand, unexpected results emerged in the variable of experience using technology, where those who were experienced tended to be more prepared to receive zakat technology than those who had just interacted with technology, although other factors such as education and income also influenced perceptions (Kasri & Yuniar, 2021; Mutamimah et al., 2021). This research explores the opportunities and challenges in the embrace of technological advancements for zakat management and identifies factors that affect the efficiency and transparency of the zakat system in the digital era. This research focuses on the relationships among the embrace of technological advancements, the reinforcement of the zakat ecosystem, and community engagement with respect to the operational efficiency and transparency of zakat institutions. With findings that show a significant influence of demographic and experiential factors on technology adoption, this study contributes to the literature on zakat and digitalization and provides a basis for the development of more inclusive and efficient zakat management strategies that support the sustainability of the zakat system in the digital era (Beik et al., 2021; Siswanti et al., 2024; Yuniar et al., 2021). This research has great significance because it offers new insights into how digital technology can be used to overcome the challenges of zakat management in the modern era. The importance of transparency and accountability in zakat management is emphasized as a key factor in building public trust in zakat institutions. In addition, findings regarding the role of experience in driving technology adoption suggest that digital training can be an effective strategy to encourage the use of technology in the zakat system. Thus, this study provides practical guidance for zakat institutions in developing digital training and education programs that are in accordance with the demographic characteristics of the community (Rahmat & Nurzaman, 2019; Soleh, 2020; Syed Yusuf et al., 2024). There are still some issues that have not been addressed in this study, such as how the specific characteristics of various digital platforms affect the perception and level of user trust in zakat institutions. Further research needs to be conducted to identify the key elements of digital platforms that are most effective in encouraging community engagement and ensuring transparency in the management of zakat funds. This study has several significant practical implications for zakat management in the digital era, especially for improving the operational efficiency and transparency of zakat institutions. First, the application of digital technology can facilitate the management and distribution of zakat funds through responsive mobile applications and interactive digital platforms. Zakat institutions can utilize this technology to optimize fund recording, monitor distribution, and help donors access information in real time. Digital training, especially for younger generations, who are more familiar with technology, can be an important strategy to increase acceptance of the use of zakat applications. This means that zakat institutions can expand the reach of services and increase public trust in a more modern zakat management process, thereby contributing to the sustainability of zakat institutions. On the basis of these findings, zakat institutions should implement a phased digitalization strategy, starting with an internal digital readiness assessment. This should be followed by the development of an easy-to-use platform and the integration of feedback mechanisms for continuous improvement. Collaboration with fintech providers will be critical to improving system efficiency, whereas digital literacy workshops targeting low-income and elderly populations will ensure inclusivity. In addition, zakat institutions should prioritize transparency and accountability by providing real-time fund tracking and reporting features. Practical Implications This study has several significant practical implications for zakat management in the digital era, especially for improving the operational efficiency and transparency of zakat institutions. First, the application of digital technology can facilitate the management and distribution of zakat funds through the use of mobile applications and responsive interactive digital platforms. Zakat institutions can utilize this technology to optimize fund recording and distribution monitoring and to help donors access information in real time. Digital training, especially for younger generations, who are more familiar with technology, can serve as an important strategy to increase acceptance of the use of zakat applications. This means that zakat institutions can expand the reach of services and increase public trust in more modern zakat management processes, thereby contributing to the sustainability of zakat institutions. Second, this study highlights the importance of paying attention to demographic characteristics such as age, income, and experience in using technology. These variables play a role in influencing the level of public acceptance of zakat technology. Zakat institutions should develop more inclusive and adaptive communication strategies by providing educational programs tailored to user characteristics. For example, older people or those with low incomes tend to have limited access to technology and require more intensive digital training. In addition, the development of features that support transparency, such as clear and real-time reporting of funds on zakat applications, can strengthen institutional accountability and build public trust in supporting broader participation and sustainability. 4.2. Limitations and future research This study has several limitations that must be considered to improve future understanding. First, the main focus of this study is the local context in Indonesia, which means that the results cannot yet be fully generalized to other regions with different digitalization characteristics. Further research needs to cover rural areas and other developing countries to obtain a broader picture of the application of technology in zakat management, which ensures the sustainability of zakat institutions across contexts. Second, this study has not reviewed in depth the specific influence of digital platform characteristics on user perceptions and trust in zakat institutions. Future research can explore key elements of digital platforms that are most effective in encouraging community involvement and ensuring transparency in fund management. Third, user adaptation to technology still requires further study, especially with respect to how government policies and regulations affect the acceptance of technology in Zakat. Future research should consider the impact of policies and the application of cutting-edge technologies such as blockchain and AI to improve the security and efficiency of zakat management, which will support the long-term sustainability of the zakat system. Longitudinal research is also needed to track changes in the perception and adoption of technology over time, provide deeper insights into the impact of technology on zakat management, and formulate long-term strategies for zakat institutions to adapt to dynamic technological developments. 5. Conclusions In conclusion, this study confirms the significant potential of the embrace of zakat technological advancements in enhancing the efficiency, transparency, and accountability of zakat management. The data suggest that the younger generation https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Arwen et al. (2026) 16 is increasingly embracing zakat technological advancements, particularly among those with higher education backgrounds. However, persistent challenges related to digital literacy and access disparities remain, especially for elderly and low-income groups. The findings indicate that the adoption of technology, the reinforcement of the zakat ecosystem, and the engagement of the community are crucial for improving operational efficiency and transparency. The research identifies the necessity of an inclusive approach tailored to the demographic characteristics of users. Implementing effective strategies to bolster digital literacy in underserved communities, in conjunction with fostering partnerships among zakat institutions, the government, and technological advancement providers, will be pivotal by means of ensuring the triumph achievements in embracing zakat technological advancements. Furthermore, ensuring that successful outcomes are achieved while embracing current technology advancements and sustainability is critical. In its entirety, the insights from this research significantly contribute to the body of literature on zakat digitization while offering strategic recommendations for zakat institutions to increase their effectiveness in collecting and distributing funds. Through the effective embrace of zakat technological advancements, zakat institutions can enhance their responsiveness to community expectations for transparency and efficiency, guaranteeing the prompt and accurate distribution of zakat to beneficiaries. Future research may concentrate on exploring policies and exemplary practices related to the embrace of zakat technological advancements, ensuring their sustainability. JSON: Name: digital_zakat_sem_tangerang Title: Structural equation modeling evaluation of digital platform adoption effects on operational efficiency and transparency of zakat collection and distribution in Tangerang, Indonesia Short Hypothesis: Inclusive adoption of digital zakat platforms together with strengthened zakat-ecosystem coordination and active community engagement causes a statistically significant increase in operational efficiency and in transparency/accountability of zakat collection and distribution compared to digital platform adoption without ecosystem reinforcement or community engagement. Related Work: Existing work has deployed mobile apps, e-wallet integrations, cloud-based MIS and pilot blockchain proofs-of-concept to digitize zakat collection and distribution; common analytic approaches are cross-sectional surveys, TAM/TPB extensions, and structural equation modeling to relate technology adoption, trust, and perceived outcomes. Reported benefits include faster transactions, lower per-transaction costs, and improved traceability, while gaps remain: most studies are localized and cross-sectional (limiting causal claims), focus on younger/urban users, and evaluate adoption intent rather than operational outcomes; platform feature-level effects (e.g., automated reporting, notifications, verification workflows) are rarely isolated; security/privacy and transaction-level integrity are discussed conceptually but seldom measured empirically; and few studies combine self-reported perception data with objective platform logs or randomized/quasi-experimental interventions to quantify causal impact. Consequently, unresolved issues include the relative contributions of pure technology adoption versus ecosystem coordination and community engagement, feature-level effectiveness, and external validity across demographic strata. Abstract: Problem: Zakat collection and distribution face inefficiencies, limited transparency, and uneven adoption of digital platforms across demographic groups. Approach: We propose a mixed quantitative causal evaluation that combines cross-sectional survey data, platform transaction logs, and a randomized cluster intervention to test how digital platform adoption, zakat-ecosystem reinforcement, and community engagement interact to affect operational efficiency and transparency. Method: Use confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM) to quantify direct and mediated effects, supplemented by difference-in-differences and randomized treatment contrasts to establish causality. Contribution: The study isolates the incremental impact of ecosystem coordination and community engagement beyond platform deployment, links perception-based measures to objective transaction metrics, and compares platform feature variants (basic donation vs automated reporting vs blockchain-anchored audit trail). Expected outcome: Quantified causal estimates of pathway strengths (path coefficients, R2), demonstration of which interventions materially improve funds-to-beneficiary metrics and transparency indicators, and evidence-based recommendations for inclusive digitalization strategies for zakat institutions. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Baseline cross-sectional survey n≈400 stratified across 13 subdistricts (demographics, technology adoption, trust, perceptions); 2) platform transaction logs from participating zakat platforms (timestamps, amounts, processing times, distribution records, verification events) over 6 months; 3) administrative distribution outcome records from Baznas (beneficiary counts, disbursement amounts, timeliness). Experimental design: cluster-randomized trial at subdistrict level with four arms (A: control — existing digital platform with basic donation UI; B: platform + ecosystem reinforcement (automated inter-institution workflows and consolidated reporting); C: platform + community engagement (digital literacy campaigns + in-app interactive notifications); D: combined B+C). Randomize at least 24 clusters (6 per arm) if feasible; pre-intervention baseline period 2 months and treatment period 6 months. Baselines for comparison: manual-collection historical baseline (pre-digital period) and current basic-digital platform (arm A). Evaluation metrics: Operational efficiency — mean transaction processing time (seconds), cost per transaction (USD/IDR), percent of collected funds disbursed to mustahik within target window (e.g., 30 days), fund leakage rate (discrepancy between collected and recorded disbursed); Transparency/accountability — availability of real-time public reporting (binary per donation), donor-reported trust score (Likert), audit-trace completeness score (proportion of transactions with end-to-end verification), number of reconciliation exceptions per 1,000 transactions. Statistical analysis: Confirmatory factor analysis for latent constructs (TA, ZE, CI, OE, T&A); SEM (PLS and covariance-based) to estimate path coefficients and mediation; difference-in-differences estimation to measure pre-post changes across arms; cluster-robust standard errors; bootstrapped significance (5,000 resamples) for path coefficients; ANOVA and post-hoc Tukey tests for arm comparisons. Ablation studies: (i) SEM re-estimated removing community engagement latent variable to assess change in R2 and path coefficients for OE and T&A; (ii) feature ablation on platform logs comparing transactions with automated reporting enabled vs disabled; (iii) compare blockchain-anchored reporting subset vs conventional reporting subset for audit-trace completeness. Robustness checks: demographic subgroup SEM (age, income, education), propensity-score weighting if noncompliance occurs, sensitivity analysis for missing outcome data using multiple imputation. Success criteria: statistically significant positive path coefficients (p<0.05) from ZE and CI to OE and T&A; treatment arm D shows greater pre-post improvements in objective metrics vs A with p<0.05 and effect sizes reported. Risk Factors and Limitations: Sampling bias: urban, smartphone-owning respondents overrepresent younger and higher-educated users limiting external validity to rural/low-income groups; Self-report bias: survey measures (trust, perceived transparency) subject to social desirability and recall error; Noncompliance and contamination: users in control clusters may adopt treated features or receive training, diluting treatment contrasts; Data linkage gaps: inability to reliably link survey respondents to transaction logs limits individual-level causal inference; Privacy and legal constraints: restrictions on sharing transaction and beneficiary data may reduce sample of usable objective metrics; Measurement limitations: operational efficiency and leakage estimates depend on administrative data quality and consistent coding across institutions; Scalability and compute: processing and secure storage of transaction logs and blockchain proofs may require infrastructure beyond local zakat institutions; Technical failure modes: platform outages, flawed implementation of automated workflows, or immature blockchain integration can produce spurious negative effects; Generalization limits: results from Tangerang may not generalize to regions with substantially different digital infrastructure, cultural norms, or regulatory regimes; Confounding policy shifts: concurrent regulatory or NGO interventions during the trial period could confound observed effects.
